data.title: Private-hire drivers, delivery workers spur growth in Singapore’s platform workforce in 2026
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The number of regular own-account workers, who operate their own business without employing any paid staff, increased by 11.4 per cent year on year to 231,900 in 2026, from 208,200 in 2025.

This marked the highest number of such workers since 2016, excluding pandemic-era highs of 248,500 in 2021 and 257,300 in 2022, a Ministry of Manpower (MOM) report showed on Friday (Nov 27).

Self-employed residents made up 11.8 per cent of Singapore’s resident workforce for the third straight year in 2026. Of these, about seven in 10 are own-account workers.

The number of platform workers – who make up one-third of regular own-account workers – also grew in 2026. There were 74,600 such workers this year, up from 71,600 in 2025.

Platform workers are defined as own-account workers who provide paid services such as ride-hail or delivery under agreements with platform operators.

Despite this rise, the proportion of platform workers as a share of employed residents remained the same as previous years, at 3 per cent.

Not enough work?

The overall share of regular own-account workers who reported that they faced challenges was largely stable year on year at 18.4 per cent in 2026, against 18.2 per cent in 2025. The main challenges that they cited were uncertainty about finding sufficient work and insufficient work.

Meanwhile, the share of platform workers facing challenges increased to 17.7 per cent in 2026, from 14.8 per cent in 2025. Higher business expenses, such as an increase in petroleum costs on the back of supply shortages, were another difficulty flagged.

Still, the proportion of own-account workers facing challenges has declined significantly since 66 per cent in 2016, when the study was first conducted, and from the pandemic-era peak of 55.1 per cent in 2021.

“The overall decline reflects continuing collective efforts from the government and tripartite partners in addressing key issues faced, such as concerns regarding healthcare, retirement and income loss in the event of work injury,” MOM added.

Flexibility and freedom

In 2026, nearly nine in 10 own-account workers, or 198,600, did it as their main job and livelihood, up from 179,200 in 2025.

Private-hire drivers and delivery workers were behind the increase in the number of platform workers in 2026, reflecting stronger demand for such services, MOM said.

There were 38,100 private-hire drivers in 2026, up from 36,000 in 2025, while the number of delivery workers rose to 16,100, from 14,700 before.

In contrast, the number of taxi drivers has been declining gradually over the longer term, to 21,000 in 2026, from 25,400 in 2022.

Some 63.5 per cent of those doing platform work as their main livelihood were seniors aged 50 or older, slightly lower than the 65.6 per cent in the year before, while 71.7 per cent were non-tertiary educated, compared with 75.7 per cent in 2025.

The survey found that nearly all regular primary own-account workers did such work on a preferred basis, for reasons such as flexibility in working hours and location, freedom to choose the work they want, and greater control over their career. 

The minority of own-account workers engaging in such work on the side could be using it to complement their main job and lifestyle, the report also suggested. Their numbers rose to 33,300 in 2026, from 29,000 in 2025.

“The flexibility and accessibility offered by platform work may continue to attract older workers transitioning into retirement or seeking alternative income sources in later career stages,” the report said.

MOM added that the enactment of the Platform Workers Act in 2025 has strengthened safeguards for such workers by addressing compensation for work-related injuries, housing and retirement adequacy, and a legal framework for representation.

data.title: ComfortDelGro to consult unions before changing fares, commissions or rentals for  drivers under new agreement
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] ComfortDelGro can no longer make decisions that affect drivers’ earnings on its taxi and private-hire Zig platform without first consulting the union, under two collective agreements signed on Friday (Nov 27).

Changes to fares, rentals or commissions will go through a consultation with the National Private Hire Vehicles Association (NPHVA) and the National Taxi Association (NTA) before they are implemented,

ComfortDelGro must give at least two weeks’ notice of adjustments to fares, the app or pilot programmes on Zig. Consultation can be skipped only in urgent cases, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and ComfortDelGro said in a joint statement.

The two associations are Platform Work Associations (PWAs) affiliated to the NTUC. The agreements, the first between a platform operator and PWAs in Singapore, take effect on Dec 1.

They build on ComfortDelGro’s formal recognition of the NPHVA and NTA in February 2025, shortly after the Platform Workers Act took effect.

The agreements also formalise Zig’s practice of giving drivers an itemised statement for every trip and payout. It shows what each fare is comprised of, including surcharges and incentives. It also shows commission, payment processing fees, Central Provident Fund contributions and net earnings.

ComfortDelGro is the first platform operator in Singapore to commit in a collective agreement to share data on drivers’ work with the PWAs. It will provide aggregated figures on earnings, online hours and completed trips.

It will also provide further information to verify earnings, monitor job trends and handle grievances.

Except in serious cases such as gross misconduct, ComfortDelGro will warn or notify drivers before suspending or removing them from the platform.

Drivers can appeal through their association and receive a written outcome with reasons. Unresolved disputes can go to the Ministry of Manpower for conciliation and, if needed, to the Industrial Arbitration Court.

Drivers who rent vehicles from Zig will be entitled to preferential commission rates. Hirers of Zig vehicles will also be covered by benefits such as a personal accident scheme and rental incentives.

ComfortDelGro will help eligible drivers apply for government-paid leave including maternity, paternity, shared parental and childcare leave. It will also offer health screening at preferential rates.

Eligible drivers who suffer permanent incapacity from an accident while doing platform work, and who qualify for work injury compensation, will get up to S$2,000 in interim relief. This is on top of the compensation required by law.

A minimum fare of S$9 also applies to ComfortRide trips on Zig. It may be reviewed as operating costs and market conditions change.

NTUC secretary-general Ng Chee Meng said every major platform operator in Singapore now recognises the PWAs. “Zig is now the first to go further and sign collective agreements with them, setting an example for the sector,” he said. He called on other operators to follow.

ComfortDelGro managing director and group chief executive Cheng Siak Kian said the agreements give the company “a stronger way to navigate” changes in the industry together with the associations.

NTA president Tan Yeo Hua said ComfortDelGro will talk to the association first when it plans changes that affect income, “so we have our say before it decides anything”.

The agreements cover NPHVA and NTA members. ComfortDelGro will sponsor six months of NTUC membership for drivers who qualify.

The company said it invests more than S$5.5 million a year in welfare programmes and incentives. When fuel prices rose after the Middle East conflict, it absorbed part of the increase.

It also introduced a temporary per-trip fee paid directly to drivers and gave taxi drivers fuel credits.

data.title: 12 years on, Lululemon’s Singapore journey comes full circle with expanded Ion Orchard store
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Tim Campbell-Scott still remembers the first item he purchased from a Lululemon store. It was a training top from the brand’s first store in Asia – at the Ion Orchard mall in Singapore – more than a decade ago.

He was based in Singapore with another company at the time, but as fate would have it, he ended up joining the Nasdaq-listed multinational athletic apparel retailer in 2017 and he has stayed ever since.

Now the market director for South-east Asia, Campbell-Scott was back at Ion Orchard earlier this month for the reopening of the brand’s flagship store. This expanded 5,821 square foot (sq ft) space – nearly double the size of the original store in the mall – on the first basement level features Singapore’s first in-store personalisation services and a dedicated community space.

In the lead-up to that Nov 11 event, Lululemon organised the “Made to Feel” pop-up event at Design Orchard, a four-day fitness and wellness activation featuring reformer pilates, yoga, community runs and training sessions led by Lululemon ambassadors and instructors.

BT Weekend sat down for coffee with Campbell-Scott to find out more about the brand’s 12-year presence in Singapore and how it is also expanding heavily in other parts of South-east Asia. 

Not many brands, especially in Singapore’s tough retail scene, last for several years, much less 12. How has the journey been like?

The time has really flown by so quickly, and it’s been amazing to see how Lululemon has grown in Singapore. The “sweat scene”, as we like to call it, has become so much bigger, and just having the opportunity to be in all of these different spaces in Singapore has been a real blessing. 

This reopened store has our new global store design concept, which pays homage to our Vancouver roots and the natural landscapes of the Pacific Northwest (in North America).

We have grown and adapted ourselves over the years to the changing consumer attitudes towards movement, wellness and activewear, and strengthening our connection with the local communities.

Outside of the stores, Lululemon has been doing many different kinds of activities and events too. What’s the thinking behind these?

Yes, it’s part of our overall strategy to build these connections with different groups of people. We had a “Training Ground” event in January at Clarke Quay where our brand ambassador, South Korea’s Physical: 100 star Amotti, was in town to conduct some classes.

We have a running club that meets regularly at one of our stores around the island. These are usually on a Sunday morning and our pacers take groups of people on a roughly 50-minute run in the vicinity.

We are not an exclusive club. We just want people to come experience what we are about, get to work out with our ambassadors, whether or not you are wearing our products. We hope that more people will want to experience what it feels like to move when they wear our products.

It’s also quite obvious there’s been a big shift towards catering for the male customer too. 

We’ve definitely seen an increase in the male demographic walking through our stores. We have dedicated zones for men and this is part of our strategy to cater to this group. 

The male guest can be a hybrid athlete who’s looking for different products, whether it’s a top that he can run or train in, or even do yoga in. Then there are the guys who want really comfortable daywear like shirts, jackets and pants where it’s still a professional look for the office but it’s not necessarily shirt-and-tie.

What are the plans for other markets in South-east Asia?

We now have nine stores in Singapore and these are quite spread out – from Jem in the West to Changi Airport’s Terminals 1 and 3 in the East. I feel like we are in the strategic places that we need to be, but there’s always room to do more. It would be naive for me to say there’s no future growth in Singapore. There’s definitely still more that we would like to do in Singapore.

As for the rest of South-east Asia, we are currently present in Malaysia and Thailand. It’s been a little over a year since we opened a roughly 4,500 sq ft store in Mega Bangna, one of the largest malls in Bangkok. We entered the Thailand market three years ago and that’s a big population where the sweat scene is still building, so there is a lot of opportunity to grow further.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson Holdings, Hongkong Land, Marco Polo Marine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 27):

Jardine Matheson Holdings (JMH) , Hongkong Land : JMH announced on Thursday that Adam Keswick – whose family controls the Jardine group – will step down from the board effective Dec 31, 2026. He will also step down from the board of Hongkong Land. JMH ended Thursday at US$60.38, up US$0.25 or 0.4 per cent, while Hongkong Land was US$0.07 or 0.8 per cent higher at US$8.53, before the announcement.

Marco Polo Marine : The marine logistics company posted on Friday a 56 per cent drop in net profit to S$21.3 million for its second half ended Sep 30, 2026, from S$47.9 million in the previous corresponding period. Revenue for H2 rose 11 per cent to S$78 million from S$70.1 million. Earnings per share stood at S$0.0055 for the half-year period, down from S$0.0128. Shares of Marco Polo Marine ended at S$0.093 on Thursday, S$0.005 or 5.7 per cent higher.

data.title: Singapore shares continue gains from Thursday, STI up 0.7%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stocks ended higher on Friday (Nov 27).

The benchmark Straits Times Index (STI) gained 0.7 per cent or 32.59 points to finish at 4,995.23.

UOL Group led the gainers on Singapore’s blue-chip index, rising 2.2 per cent or S$0.16 to S$7.44.

The worst performer among STI constituents was Seatrium , which fell 1.5 per cent or S$0.02 to S$1.29, continuing its decline for the week.

The three local banks ended higher. DBS gained 0.5 per cent or S$0.30 to S$66.15, OCBC rose 0.7 per cent or S$0.19 to S$26.80, and UOB was up 1 per cent or S$0.37 at S$35.81.

Within the iEdge Singapore Next 50 Index, ULTRAGREEN AI USD was the top gainer, rising 7 per cent or US$0.025 to US$0.38; Yangzijiang Financial was the biggest decliner, falling 2.9 per cent or S$0.006 to S$0.199.

Across the broader market, gainers outnumbered losers 418 to 166, with 1.2 billion securities worth S$1.6 billion having changed hands.

Key regional indices were positive. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index gained 2.1 per cent, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 2.1 per cent, South Korea’s Kospi was up 4.3 per cent and the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI advanced 1.2 per cent. The US markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday.

Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, said: “Friday’s rally was a much more enthusiastic response, but it came after selling pressure had already grown substantial and positioning had become increasingly defensive.”

He added: “Beijing has taken the unusual step of delivering a market-support message in the middle of the trading day, offering battered Chinese equities a welcome reprieve.

“Technology shares led a spectacular recovery as investors responded to renewed promises of state-backed buying and measures designed to encourage longer-term investment.

“With economic fundamentals still struggling and Washington tightening access to advanced AI chips, investors must decide whether Beijing has delivered a genuine turning point or simply interrupted another round of selling.”

data.title: Why a professional baseline for HR is a reasonable expectation
data.description:
IF THE pace of change feels faster, it is because it is. New artificial intelligence systems are arriving at speed and organisations are moving them from experiments into everyday workflows.

In conversations with business and human resources (HR) leaders, I hear the same questions: Which tasks should be automated? How should decisions be made? And how must operating models evolve to ensure that technology improves performance without leaving people behind?

For workers, these are not abstract questions. Familiar tasks may disappear while new ones emerge. Skills built over many years may no longer be enough.

The result is a mixture of anticipation and anxiety, particularly when change affects a person’s livelihood, career prospects and sense of what lies ahead.

Technology is only one part of this transformation. Singapore is also facing rapid population ageing.

In 2026, citizens aged 65 and above made up 21.4 per cent of Singapore’s citizen population, placing the country above the threshold commonly used to define a super-aged society.

As more people remain in the workforce for longer, employers will need to redesign jobs, provide flexible work arrangements and build workplaces where different generations can contribute and learn from one another.

The regulatory landscape is also evolving. Parliament has passed the Workplace Fairness Act and the accompanying dispute-resolution legislation, both of which are scheduled to take effect at the end of 2027.

Employers will need stronger systems for fair employment decisions, grievance handling and documentation. What was once guided mainly by tripartite norms will increasingly carry statutory obligations and consequences.

Taken together, these shifts raise a straightforward question: What should employers and workers be able to expect from the professionals who advise on decisions that carry legal risk and can alter working lives?

This question lies at the heart of the recent report by the Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development, which sets out five recommendations to strengthen Singapore’s human capital capabilities.

One proposal has attracted particular attention: from Jul 1, 2028, organisations with more than 200 employees will need at least one HR professional certified at the Institute for Human Resource Practitioners (IHRP) Certified Professional level or higher.

Recognised equivalent accreditations may also qualify, subject to applicable bridging requirements.

These concerns are understandable. A certificate cannot capture everything that makes a good HR professional. It cannot fully measure empathy, courage or judgment, nor predict how someone will respond when an employee’s role is at risk or a business faces a painful restructuring.

Neither should experienced practitioners without certification be dismissed as incapable; many have built deep expertise over decades.

However, the limits of certification are not an argument against a professional baseline.

When someone advises on employment rights, workplace fairness, grievances or restructuring, employers and workers should have confidence that the individual has demonstrated a recognised foundation of HR knowledge, ethics and professional judgment.

A baseline should also not be mistaken for a one-off examination that divides the capable from the incapable. Professional certification should be a continuing commitment: a standard that evolves with business, technology, regulation and workforce expectations.

IHRP’s framework is anchored in its Body of Competencies, which was first introduced in 2016 and subsequently refreshed in 2020 and 2024 through engagement with business and HR leaders, tripartite partners and the wider ecosystem.

Some have pointed out that experience matters more. Indeed, experience remains indispensable. It deepens perspective and helps practitioners recognise patterns that no textbook can teach.

Yet, experience can also harden into familiar assumptions. Pairing it with an evolving professional standard gives practitioners reason to test what they think they know, update their knowledge and keep their judgment current.

There is a broader point here about the standing of HR I hope can be further debated. When people think of the professions on which society depends, they often cite medicine, law, accountancy and engineering.

HR should be part of this conversation too. HR practitioners apply specialised knowledge, exercise professional judgment, uphold ethical standards and advise on decisions with serious consequences for individuals and organisations.

Professional recognition should reflect this level of responsibility. This requirement is an important step towards positioning HR alongside other recognised professions – a profession that our community can be proud of.

IHRP, for its part, has work to do. Certification must remain rigorous, accessible and relevant. The standards must keep pace with generative AI, flexible work, new workforce models and the responsible use of people data.

Recertification must reflect genuine professional development rather than become a passive pay-to-maintain exercise. Together with learning and ecosystem partners, we must give practitioners practical ways to learn, find mentors, exchange experience and support one another.

Ultimately, the measure of professionalisation will not be the number of certificates issued. It will be whether employment practices become fairer, workforce planning improves, difficult decisions are handled more responsibly and trust in HR grows.

A professional baseline cannot guarantee these outcomes. However, at a time when employers face increasingly complex and consequential decisions, it is a reasonable place to start.

The writer is chief executive officer of the IHRP

data.title: McLaren Automotive aims to widen audience with planned SUV
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The next wave of customers for British ultra luxury carmaker McLaren Automotive could well come from the likes of the latest K-pop stars: Younger, Asian and female.

That is because the carmaker is now embarking on a new 10-year plan, which includes expanding its model range to include a sports utility vehicle (SUV) for the first time, marking a major departure from its history.

Henrik Wilhelmsmeyer, McLaren Automotive’s chief commercial officer, said: “I think we will see very different customers going forward. Today there are a lot of customers with a household of more than two people, who would love to enjoy a McLaren without leaving others behind.”

Sport cars to sport utility

Wilhelmsmeyer confirmed that an SUV is in the works, but provided no specific details. Media reports say the car could be launched as soon as 2028.

In an interview with The Business Times, he said: “We see globally that (the SUV segment is) one of the fastest-growing segments still, and that holds true in Asia as well as Europe and the US.”

While high-performance cars will remain an important part of the business, Wilhelmsmeyer admits that supercars only have relevance to a “certain audience”.

“A supercar, by definition, is built for one purpose. An SUV certainly supports different use cases, and that makes it more relevant to more people,” he added.

McLaren Automotive was founded in 2010 as part of McLaren Group, which includes the Formula 1 team McLaren Racing. Since then, the Woking-based manufacturer has focused on high-performance, two-door, two-seat supercars.

Globally, traditional buyers of supercars are older men, typically above 50. As it has with other luxury carmakers, an SUV will help boost McLaren’s appeal to younger buyers and women.

“A fast-growing age band for us is between 20 (and) 30 years old, and we see more clients coming from the tech industry…whereas maybe the previous generation has taken an entire generation to create that wealth, we see this now happening way earlier, and customers are approaching us at a much younger age than ever before.”

Wilhelmsmeyer said another aim is to draw more female buyers to the brand. While he did not link the new SUV to those buyers directly, historically SUVs have had more appeal to women, even in the ultra-luxury segment.

In Asia-Pacific, outside of China, Japan is a key market with an established supercar-buying audience and large automotive collector market, but South Korea is also fast rising as one of its “most dynamic markets that has a comparatively younger, new audience that is just discovering the brand”.

Less with more

For low volume ultra-luxury carmakers such as McLaren, production is about balancing output, profitability and exclusivity, since flooding the market with too many cars will reduce residual values, alienating existing customers.

In recent years, McLaren has relooked its strategy, reducing output by building only according to demand in order to preserve resale values and prevent sales cannibalisation.

It has also focused on higher margin per car by offering more customisation options through its bespoke division, McLaren Special Operations (MSO).

In 2025, McLaren produced around 2,000 cars, down from 3,300 in 2024. In 2025, rivals Aston Martin manufactured 5,448, Bentley had 10,131 while Ferrari produced 13,640.

All these brands have introduced SUVs in recent years.

Like its competitors, a new SUV will likely mean McLaren must increase its annual production numbers, although Wilhelmsmeyer said there are no new volume targets set as yet and its production strategy remains the same for now.

“Now, the production volume is not predefined. Our clear strategic direction is that we want to be a demand-led business. This means we only want to build cars for a customer. We don’t want to build cars on stock,” he said.

In September, McLaren announced a fresh £500 million (US$655.5 million) funding from its new owner, L’imad, the sovereign fund of Abu Dhabi. The money will be used to build a second factory alongside its existing one in the UK to facilitate the model portfolio expansion.

Formerly, McLaren was majority owned by Bahrain Mumtalakat, the sovereign fund of Bahrain. CYVN, an Abu Dhabi-based transport investment firm, acquired Mumtalakat’s stake in the business in 2024, and was itself folded into L’imad in early 2026.

L’imad’s planned investments in the automaker amount to £1.5 billion over the next five years.

Part of the investments will also be used to expand MSO.

“MSO strategically is our focus for us. It is more relevant to grow the value per car that we sell than the absolute number of cars…the more you personalise and individualise a car, the longer it takes to build, and the less you can do of them,” said Wilhelmsmeyer.

data.title: Vietnamese partners of Trump Organization plan Trump Tower in Hanoi, sources say
data.description:
[HANOI] Vietnamese business partners of the Trump Organization are planning a skyscraper in Hanoi, three people with knowledge of the new project said.

It is one of three Trump-branded projects in the works in the South-east Asian nation.

A US$1.5 billion Trump-branded golf complex is being developed near Hanoi by local partners of the Trump Organization. A separate Trump Tower is planned in Ho Chi Minh City, people involved with the project have said.

All the projects are being developed at no cost to the Trump Organization, which earns money from the use of its brand, operating fees and property sales, one person with direct knowledge of the plans said.

Vietnamese government officials met the Trump Organization’s partners, which include Kinh Bac City Development Holding, on Thursday (Nov 26) to discuss the Hanoi project, according to two of the sources.

The meeting took place shortly after Washington announced possible new tariffs of up to 35 per cent on Vietnam, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade deal is struck, they said.

One of the people said the project was first submitted to the government in May and that it had not yet received approval.

All sources declined to be named as the information was not public. The plans for a new Trump Tower in Hanoi are being reported here for the first time.

The Trump Organization, US President Donald Trump’s family business, was not immediately available for comment outside US working hours. Vietnam’s government and Kinh Bac City Development did not immediately respond to requests for comment. REUTERS

data.title: Is it lights out for Singapore’s night-time economy?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore does well in attracting visitors for major events, from Formula 1 and concerts to conferences and exhibitions.

Liu Dongjie, who is pursuing a Master of Business Administration at Nanyang Technological University (NTU), recounts that pop star Taylor Swift’s six sold-out shows in 2024 were a “trigger” for his overseas friends to visit the city-state.

But when they went to Clarke Quay – Singapore’s iconic riverside nightlife enclave – after the concert, most restaurants were already closed. The group found the late-night options limited.

“They just came for the event,” he says. “There is no retention for Singapore.”

By all accounts, the Republic’s nightlife sector has turned moribund.

The operating revenue of pubs, nightclubs, discotheques, dance clubs and karaoke lounges fell by more than half in the last decade, from S$674.7 million in 2015 to S$284.7 million in 2022, based on a white paper released by the Singapore Nighttime Business Association (SNBA) in September this year.

The night-time economy “is struggling, if I’ll be honest”, says SNBA president Danny Loong. “I think we are trying to adjust to the new realities.”

No place like home

Singapore’s nights used to be livelier. From the 1980s to the 2000s, nightclubs and supper spots kept people out well past midnight. But the city’s club scene has since thinned.

The iconic Zouk remains, albeit at a different location, but several other well-known venues – such as The Butter Factory, St James Power Station and Shanghai Dolly – have closed down.

Most malls close by 10 pm, limiting after-work shopping options, while drinking establishments must stop serving alcohol before midnight.

At the same time, any night-time buzz needs people who are willing to head out.

Liu and his classmates learnt from interviews with NTU students that some prefer gathering in their dormitories – where they can drink more cheaply, play their own music, and avoid the transport costs of getting home after public buses and trains have stopped operating.

Businesses are “competing with a behavioural default of staying at home”, notes Dr Tan Kim Lim, head of James Cook University Singapore’s Centre for International Trade and Business in Asia.

He adds that the Covid-19 pandemic reinforced this habit, while digital technology makes at-home entertainment options more attractive and convenient.

Another hurdle that SNBA identified is the expense of getting home after a night out. The consumer price index for point-to-point transport services was 45 per cent higher in September 2026 than in September 2021.

This increased cost adds to the price of an after-dark jaunt – making it less appealing to some to head out late.

Rethinking nightlife

One bright spot is that dining out remains popular with Singapore residents. In a 2025 Knight Frank-Ipsos survey, 66 per cent of local respondents selected dining as a preferred leisure activity, compared with 10 per cent who chose clubbing and nightlife. 

The F&B industry is thus a stalwart propping up late-night pastimes. But more eateries may not be enough to sustain the sector.

Kent Teo, CEO of events firm Invade, describes F&B as a “super red ocean” – a loss-making segment, with home-grown businesses struggling to compete in a market saturated with foreign brands.

For Loong, the solution is not simply to bring back clubs and bars. “These days, it’s about building experience, placemaking, place management and combining all these different parts together to make it more vibrant,” he says.

That broader remit is reflected in SNBA’s recent rebrand – until August, it was called the Singapore Nightlife Business Association – and its recommendations.

Against this backdrop, SNBA’s precinct approach aims to draw people out by bringing local businesses, cultural activities and public spaces together.

Lewis Lim, associate professor of marketing practice at NTU’s Nanyang Business School, supervised Liu and several other MBA students on a project conducted in collaboration with SNBA.

Informed in part by the students’ research, the SNBA white paper proposes broadening the night economy beyond bars and clubs to include shopping, creative industries and cultural activities, among others.

It also calls for better late-night transport, a “night pass” offering credits for transport and ticketed experiences, a national night-time economy office, as well as distinctive precincts including Holland Village, Clarke Quay, Orchard Road and Kampong Glam.

These proposals would complement other efforts to enliven Singapore’s precincts after dark.

In August, the government formalised such measures trialled for a year in Boat Quay, Clarke Quay and Upper Circular Road, including later alcohol trading hours and the resumption of Circular Road closures for events. 

The Singapore Tourism Board’s Orchard Road Rejuvenation Initiative, which was unveiled in May, similarly supports industry-led night programming, including curated markets and extended operating hours tied to events.

Loong, the SNBA president, thinks transport and precinct development are among the proposals that can realistically be pursued. Talks with the authorities on transport are under way, he says, declining to elaborate beyond describing them as “constructive”.

Precincts as multipliers

The precinct proposal is central to SNBA’s case that Singapore can compete for the night-time dollar on unique offerings rather than price.

Home-grown brands and creative talent, the white paper says, can become “destination assets” that help define what experiencing Singapore after dark means.

The organisation argues that neighbourhoods should be places for Singaporeans to enjoy and identify with, which will draw visitors seeking to experience what locals do.

According to the white paper, successful precincts need strong identities, which can be built through coordinated programming, attractive public spaces, cultural activity and collaboration among government, communities and businesses.

That identity would come from a mix of local restaurants, bars, cafes, entertainment concepts, music venues, cultural businesses, retailers and lifestyle operators.

The NTU researchers describe what that mix should offer visitors: places to eat, listen to music and stay late, alongside hotels, transport and safe waiting spaces. 

A walkable precinct would let people move between them without taking a private-hire ride to continue their night elsewhere, easing some concerns about transport costs.

This mix can also make it less risky for businesses to extend their hours.

NTU’s Prof Lim says one operator may hesitate to stay open late alone, but if nearby businesses do the same, their combined offerings can give people more reason to visit.

“There’s an ecosystem there. One kind of business makes another more attractive. It’s a multiplier effect.”

Home-grown businesses can anchor precincts with offerings and experiences that overseas visitors are less likely to find in their home countries, notes Musa Fazal, chief policy and operating officer of the Singapore Business Federation (SBF).

Supporting local businesses

SNBA’s Loong also hopes landlords will consider the tenant mix.

“Everybody plays a part in building up our culture and creating space for something more uniquely Singapore,” he says. “If we are going to be uniquely Singapore, then we have to have Singapore brands.”

But these may struggle in a crowded real estate market where foreign brands, such as restaurant chains from mainland China, can pay record rents and crowd out smaller players.

Noting that “shopping malls have become ‘copy-and-paste’, because whoever can pay stays”, Invade’s Teo suggests building lifestyle destinations out of empty school compounds in the Singapore Land Authority’s land bank.

For instance, the former Nan Chiau High School campus at Kim Yam Road has been reinvented as New Bahru, which houses home-grown food, retail, art, wellness and design brands. Evening offerings include a coffee-shop-cum-taproom, cultural gatherings and live performances.

Similarly, Hong Kong’s PMQ is a former police housing complex turned creative hub, while Taipei’s Songshan Cultural and Creative Park used to be a tobacco factory.

Even so, Teo acknowledges that such spaces lack malls’ ready-made amenities, meaning that operators would have to invest in facilities and renovations.

On top of that, rents would need to be effectively subsidised to offset those costs – and that still does not guarantee the spaces would draw a night-time crowd.

“If people are not even coming out, then we don’t need to talk about rental at all,” he says.

Therefore, he also calls for efforts to improve existing businesses, such as Clarke Quay’s eateries and live performance venues, which are “not exactly doing too well”.

“If we want to focus on the night-time economy, we need to focus on what is already here,” he says.

Prof Lim adds that government support may also be needed to “help some sectors for the greater good”, especially in enabling small businesses to become more established.

Uphill effort

In August, SNBA partnered government agency Enterprise Singapore, merchants and other stakeholders to test its pitch for distinctive night-time precincts in the expat enclave of Holland Village. 

Teo from Invade put on a festival dubbed Village Encounters, which ran for a weekend from 4 to 10 pm. The event featured games, workshops and family activities, with DJs and roving street acts and other performances later in the evening.

Seeing dining and live music as ways to build on Holland Village’s neighbourhood character, SNBA plans to work with partners on at least four more projects to develop selected precincts over the next two years.

Teo says the event recorded 26,265 visits – that is 2.6 to 5.3 times the usual traffic of 5,000 to 10,000 visits on a normal weekend, based on his team’s estimate.

Village Encounters also drew people beyond Holland Village’s regular visitors. Invade’s post-event survey of attendees shows that 45.8 per cent said it was their first visit to the enclave, or that they had visited only once or twice in the past year.

More than half said they had spent over S$20 at local F&B or retail businesses. And while 91.9 per cent of the 208 respondents said they would probably or definitely return to Holland Village within three months, actual return visits were not tracked.

Business owners tell The Business Times that results have been mixed.

Despite not participating in Village Encounters, pet store Fur saw its sales rise during the festival weekend. But Donald Kng, co-founder and CEO of parent company Vetreska, remarks that he cannot link the increase to the event.

Olivier Dyens, owner of Italian restaurant La Nonna, estimates that sales rose 15 to 20 per cent during the event, with till takings covering promotional voucher redemptions.

Yet, Wala Wala Cafe Bar owner Stanley Yeo describes the sales impact at his well-known establishment as marginal, even though some visitors who came for complimentary mocktails also ordered food.

Still, he takes a longer view of the event crowd. “There is value in simply getting people back into Holland Village.”

He adds: “They may not necessarily come into Wala Wala that particular weekend, but seeing the area and the businesses here can remind them that we are still around and give them a reason to return another time.”

Loong calls the event “just a starting point” – a showcase that supports SNBA’s plans to develop more night-time precincts in 2027.

He acknowledges that getting malls, shophouse businesses, retailers, eateries and entertainment venues to work together will take time, but he believes that regular events can give them more opportunities to do so.

Bottoms up

Reviving Singapore’s nightlife is a challenge with high stakes.

Beyond the fate of individual night-time establishments, quieter nights can be a drag on the broader economy, notes NTU’s Prof Lim. He says Singapore is missing out – for now – on an opportunity to encourage longer stays and capture more visitor spending.

Visitors stayed for an average of 3.48 days in 2025, based on Singapore Tourism Board data. If that is roughly three nights, Prof Lim estimates that one more night would extend the average stay by about a third, potentially bringing in significantly more tourism receipts.

“There’s a lot of money that can be earned,” he says, especially since daytime attractions offer little for business travellers who spend sunlit hours at conferences or exhibitions.

At the same time, the Singapore dollar goes further across the border, and Johor Bahru can tempt Singaporean night owls with a plethora of late-night activities – from affordable massages to go-karting – that are harder to come by in the Republic.

The opening of the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link in 2027 adds to the pressure. An SBF study estimates that the new cross-border connection could lead to a net S$290 million increase in annual spending flowing out of Singapore and across the Causeway.

SBF’s Musa tells BT that preparations to deal with the heightened competition should begin early, particularly where businesses need time to adjust.

“The objective is not to prevent cross-border spending – greater connectivity will naturally give consumers more choice,” he says. “It is to ensure Singapore businesses can compete on their strengths and capture opportunities in a larger, more integrated market.”

On the home front, Loong points to the recent formation of an alliance co-chaired by SNBA and SBF that brings together trade associations for the restaurant, hotel and retail industries.

“We cannot work in silos anymore,” says Loong. “You’ve got to have everybody in.”

data.title: Global economy risks hangover as growth over-reliant on AI boom: India chief economic adviser
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The global economy may be posting strong headline growth, but much of it perches atop the pinnacle of artificial intelligence – a bubble that may already have well begun to deflate.

Speaking at the Asia Future Summit on Friday (Nov 27), the chief economic adviser to the Indian government, Anantha Nageswaran, cautioned against taking post-pandemic economic resilience for granted.

“There is a sense of fragility attached to these growth numbers because they have been somewhat disproportionately reliant on one particular sector and all the capital expenditure associated with that,” he said.

“(Growth) has not necessarily percolated down to vast segments of the population… and there are also financial system vulnerabilities that are built up,” he added, and stressed the need to prepare for a potential post-bubble fallout.

He made the remarks during a panel discussion at SPH Media’s annual thought leadership conference, which returned for its fifth edition this year.

For the first time, it was jointly presented by the media organisation’s key news titles: The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

OCBC is the presenting sponsor, with Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

Nageswaran was part of a panel discussion, moderated by BT senior correspondent Ben Paul, titled “Are we headed for a global crisis? How will Asia’s economies respond?”

The other three panellists were: Akmal Nasir, Malaysia’s Minister of Economy; Guo Shan, partner at Hutong Research; and Loh Boon Chye, Singapore Exchange (SGX) group CEO.

Asked about AI’s long-term impacts on productivity, Nageswaran replied that the real question was not just whether such gains accrue, but also to whom they do.

“If the productivity gains accrue predominantly to owners of capital – but not to owners of labour – and if there is widespread labour displacement that happens… then it will not be an enduring productivity gain,” he said.

Pointing to the risks of financial destabilisation arising from the web of interwoven financing that characterises today’s AI sector, he added that a more important question was how to calculate productivity gains that are adjusted for the potential risks unleashed by AI models.

Diversify risks, not just portfolios

The risks of overconcentration were also highlighted by SGX’s Loh, who cautioned that a diversified portfolio did not necessarily translate into diversified risks.

Loh framed the AI debate around three questions:

  • whether it fundamentally changes the economy and lives;
  • whether investor capital generates adequate returns; and
  • who benefits from the potential returns.

Acknowledging that the US remains the biggest market and an enduring one, he added that opportunities abound around Asia as well.

But while opportunity can create economic value, it does not necessarily lead to investment returns, he cautioned, noting that risk could increase with continued geographical concentration.

Still, he maintained that he was not seeing signs that investors were oblivious to their overall AI exposure or the concentration risks in their portfolios.

Of chips and China

Turning to China, Guo said that the latest developments surrounding US restriction on AI chips could accelerate an adjustment in the sector, bringing forward the expected demand-supply rebalancing to next year, ahead of the previously anticipated 2028.

The restrictions could affect up to 30 per cent of the demand in the chip industry, she said, as many of China’s hyperscalers rely on overseas data centres. This would also prompt China to accelerate its domestic production, she added.

Guo does not expect Beijing to respond with another round of economic stimulus, noting that China’s economy is still on track to meet Beijing’s annual growth targets.

There is no urgency for any stimulus; rather, the central bank has been focusing on fiscal prevention, she continued.

Guo also pointed to signs that Beijing is seeking to play a more active role in stabilising the global economy, including by addressing concerns over China’s large trade surplus.

She noted that China has publicly pledged to pursue what it calls “international circulation” – a shift she said is arguably the first time China is seriously looking at its international role and how it can be a more responsible player in the global economy.

“Beijing sees that the global market has to be (integrated). We have to stabilise the supply chain so that everybody will enjoy a better business environment.”

She noted that this would involve three things for China: importing more, maintaining exports and encouraging its firms to expand overseas. She added that this approach is reminiscent of Japan’s efforts to rebalance its trade in the 1980s.

One common factor that would drive these three developments is the renminbi’s appreciation, added Guo.

“I’m looking at the renminbi to stabilise in the next year but, in the long term – we’re talking towards 2035 – we’re probably looking at the renminbi to appreciate by 40 per cent,” she said.

Malaysia turns to value creation

Malaysia, meanwhile, is seeking to capture more value from the AI boom by moving up the semiconductor supply chain, said Akmal.

While the country has traditionally been known for chip testing and packaging, it is now looking to develop higher-value capabilities further up the chain.

The government is also becoming more selective about data centre investments, with closer scrutiny of their energy and water use.

The economic spillover of such investments should extend beyond real estate and construction, and into helping build up Malaysia’s AI capabilities and those of the wider region, he added.

The Malaysian minister concluded: “We cannot build our economic strength on geopolitical rivalries… we want to be part of the solution in this very challenging world (and) definitely we need to preserve our reputation.”

By contrast, India has had relatively little exposure to the market-led AI boom, said Nageswaran, pointing to the absence of listed Indian companies among the major beneficiaries of the investment surge.

He was responding to an audience question on India’s limited presence in the AI discourse despite its established software industry.

But this could also leave the country less exposed to a potential correction, he noted.

“It also means that, because India was not part of the party, it would not be part of the hangover,” he said, contending that the party was “more or less over”.
